summary: Likelihood Language (ages 9-10, Mathematics/Probability): children learn to USE and justify the words impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain to describe how probable everyday events and chance-device outcomes are, before any numbers. The teaching aim is correct use in context — mapping each word onto the composition of a situation (how many of each outcome), reserving 'certain'/'impossible' for the true endpoints and using the graded middle for everything else. This is the gateway to the 0-to-1 scale and to comparing likelihoods. Core activity is open dialogue where the child generates and repairs their own wording against outcomes that push back; a live likelihood line/strip and sorting tasks are strong supports, and a tap-to-reveal reference scene can accompany them.
misconceptions: Treating 'even chance' as meaning 'any situation with two possible outcomes' (e.g. calling a 1-red / 5-blue draw 'even chance' because there are two colours)
Collapsing the graded words to guarantees — 'likely' taken to mean it will definitely happen, 'unlikely' that it definitely won't
Confusing 'impossible' (cannot happen, probability 0) with 'very unlikely' (rare but possible) — e.g. calling a rare draw 'impossible'
Judging likelihood by personal preference or wishful thinking rather than by how many of each outcome there are

activities.title: The Chance-master's bag: say it, then watch it happen
steps: Look into a bag you can see holds mostly red counters (e.g. 7 red and 3 blue) with the composition visible.
Before any draw, say in words how likely a red draw is and WHY, grounding the reason in the numbers ('most of them are red') rather than wanting red.

When you declare red 'certain', watch the game-master take out and show a blue counter (picked on purpose, or by drawing until one appears, because a single random draw will usually be red), then repair your word: was red certain, or only likely? Explain the difference.

Answer the opposite trap: the game-master suggests 'landing on 7 with this ordinary 1–6 die is only very unlikely, isn't it?' — decide whether 7 is very unlikely (rare but possible) or impossible (cannot happen at all), and say why.
Describe a green draw ('there are no green counters'), and a 'red or blue' draw ('only those two colours exist'), choosing and justifying a word for each.
Reject vague answers: if you say '50-50', be ready for 'but there are 7 red and 3 blue — is that even?' and recount to decide.
activities.insight: Each likelihood word corresponds to how many of each outcome there are; 'likely' is not a guarantee and 'impossible' (cannot happen at all) is stronger than 'very unlikely' (rare but possible). 'Even chance' requires equal numbers, not merely two possible outcomes.

activities.title: Physical likelihood line: peg real events and justify
steps: Set up a washing line or paper strip labelled impossible → unlikely → even chance → likely → certain.

Peg everyday, personally-meaningful events onto it, saying your placement aloud: 'it will get dark tonight', 'it will snow in July', 'I'll flip heads', 'the sun will rise tomorrow' (for the weather and daylight events, think about where you live: snow in July is likely in some southern places, and near the poles there are times with no sunset or no sunrise).
Move to structured chance devices where composition is inspectable — bags of counters, spinners with equal and unequal sections — and peg outcomes from those.
Place at least one deliberately unequal situation (7 red/3 blue; a spinner with one big section) and justify why it is NOT an even chance.
Say out loud the reason for each placement, referring to how many of each outcome there are.
activities.insight: Events can be ordered along a graded scale from impossible to certain, and placement is decided by composition, not by preference — unequal situations sit away from 'even chance'.

activities.title: Live likelihood strip with an adjustable bag
steps: Drop an event card onto a 0-to-1 likelihood strip and SAY the word that fits before confirming.
Change the number of red vs blue counters (e.g. with a slider) and watch which word best fits shift as the composition changes.
Remove the blue counters one at a time and predict, then say, which word changes and why ('likely' sliding toward 'certain' as blue is removed).
Always voice the word yourself rather than only reading the suggested-word zone.
activities.insight: The word that fits a situation depends on and moves with the composition; as favourable outcomes dominate, the likelihood slides toward 'certain', and only when none of the other outcome remains is it 'certain' (and the absent outcome 'impossible').

activities.title: Sort and order events (recognition check)
steps: Sort event cards into five groups: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain.
Order a set of events along the scale from least to most likely.
Judge deliberately tricky distractors, e.g. a two-colour but 1-vs-5 draw offered as 'even chance', and decide whether the label is right.
For each card you place, add a spoken or written reason comparing how many of each outcome there are.
activities.insight: Recognising which word fits is a useful step, but the real target is correct, justified use — distractors built from common misconceptions reveal whether the word is being applied for the right reason.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reference scene (worked examples)
steps: Browse events arranged along a likelihood line and tap each to reveal the correct word and the numeric reason behind it.
Use this as a reference or worked-example companion when checking your own reasoning after attempting an event yourself.
Try to name the word yourself first, then tap to compare with the revealed answer and reason.
activities.insight: Seeing worked reasons (why red is likely but not certain, why green is impossible) models the count-based justification expected of the child's own answers.

checkQuestion: Put in front of the child a bag holding 7 red and 3 blue counters (composition visible), and read out four events: 'I pull out a red', 'I pull out a blue', 'I pull out a green', 'I pull out a red or a blue'. Ask them to describe each using probability words — certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible — and to say WHY for each. Then ask them to place the four events on a strip from impossible to certain. Listen for the words used correctly and justified by the composition; do not offer options or expect a number.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correct USE: 'red' = likely (most but not all are red), 'blue' = unlikely (some but few), 'green' = impossible (there are none), 'red or blue' = certain (only those two colours exist). Justifications should refer to how many of each colour there are, and the strip should order them impossible(green) → unlikely(blue) → likely(red) → certain(red-or-blue).
